title: Ageing well
hookLine: a retirement plan that's all rest, and an old monk who kept his practice when told he could stop
tomorrow: work, money, family, body, age: what ties them all together?

lines: A BEACH CHAIR, AN EMPTY AFTERNOON.
cards: Retirement ads show a beach chair and a long, empty afternoon, as if the goal of a life were finally to stop. The suttas tell of Mahakassapa, one of the Buddha's great disciples, grown old. His rag robes are heavy.
He lives in the forest and walks for alms. And the Buddha himself tells him: you're old now, Kassapa. Wear the lighter robes householders give, accept their invitations to meals, and live near me.
Permission to ease up, from the teacher. What does the old monk say?

teach.b: Kassapa, gently, says no. He has long lived in the forest, eaten alms food, worn rag robes, and he gives two reasons for keeping on. One: it's a pleasant way for him to live, here and now.

teach.h: FOR HIMSELF, AND FOR THOSE AFTER.
teach.b: Two: compassion for those who come later, who might see an old monk still practicing and take heart. And the Buddha says: good, Kassapa, good.
Notice that both answers are honored. The Buddha's offer was kind; the old cart deserves straps. Kassapa's answer was also kind, toward himself and toward people he'd never meet.
Ageing well, here, isn't about refusing help or about stopping. It's keeping one practice for life because it still feeds you, and because someone younger is watching.
Help where it fits, and practice where it still fits, side by side. The Buddha didn't insist, and Kassapa didn't scorn the offer.
Now a round with the week behind us. Rest: lying down near the work, meaning to rise. Not sick in mind: the body aches, the mind isn't dragged.
Care for the sick: whoever would care for me. Breathe with it: soft around the ache. The old cart: strapped with care, still on the road.
The messenger: a gray hair, welcomed.
Kassapa carries all six into old age.

how: Many elderly Buddhists keep up daily practices such as chanting, offering and meditation, and monasteries honor senior monastics who continue to practice into old age.

o: retiring from all effort to enjoy a quiet rest
dyeing gray hair and hiding signs of getting older
keeping one practice for life, for yourself and those after

games.q: the old monk's answer — tap the pairs.
p: lighter robes, meals, live near me
a pleasant way to live, here and now
compassion for those who come later

s: the Buddha ordered Kassapa to keep his hard practices in old age
the Buddha offered him an easier life; Kassapa chose to keep on.
Kassapa kept his practice partly out of compassion for later generations
so those who come after might take heart from his example.
in the sutta to Nakulapita, the Buddha promised a sick body would heal
the line was a training: the body sick, the mind not sick.

games.q: your grandfather, slower now, says he'll quit his morning walk because 'what's the point at my age?' what does Kassapa's story offer?
o: agree; old age is the time to stop everything and rest.
keep one practice that still feeds you; someone younger may be watching.
push him to walk farther, to prove age doesn't matter.
games.why: Kassapa kept his practice for his own well-being and out of compassion for those after him; the Buddha approved.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper, and write by hand one small practice you'd like to keep for the rest of your life: a breath before meals, a kind word at night, a walk.
Write it plainly, then hold the paper and read it once, slowly, to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Ageing well: keeping one practice for life, for your own good and for those who come after, with help welcomed where it fits.

carryVoice: The line to keep: into old age, one practice carried all the way. Eight of nine.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 16.5 (Jinna Sutta: the Buddha invites the aged Mahakassapa to wear householders' robes, accept invitations and stay near him; Kassapa gives two reasons for continuing: his own pleasant dwelling here and now, and compassion for later generations; the Buddha approves)
